content: Individuals who require long-term bladder drainage often face complications such as catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTIs) and other related issues. The objective of this research was to evaluate whether specific catheter management strategies, including the route of catheter insertion and the use of antibiotics, are more effective in terms of reducing complications, improving quality of life, and being cost-effective for adults and children who require long-term catheterisation. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register as of September 28, 2011. Additionally, reference lists of identified studies were reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomised and quasi-randomised trials that compared different catheter policies for long-term use, defined as more than 14 days, in both adults and children. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. The data were processed according to the Cochrane Handbook guidelines. When trial data were incomplete, clarification was sought from the original authors. In some cases, incidence-density rates (IDR) and incidence-density differences (IDD) were calculated to provide additional insights. A total of eight trials, involving 504 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These included four cross-over trials and four parallel-group randomised controlled trials. However, only two of the six pre-specified comparisons were addressed in these studies. Four trials compared the use of antibiotic prophylaxis with administering antibiotics only when clinically indicated. Among patients using intermittent catheterisation, the findings were inconsistent regarding the impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on symptomatic UTIs. Only one study demonstrated a significant reduction in UTI frequency in favor of prophylaxis. For patients with indwelling urethral catheters, one small trial reported fewer episodes of symptomatic UTIs in the group receiving prophylactic antibiotics. Another four trials compared antibiotic prophylaxis with administering antibiotics only when microbiologically indicated. For patients using intermittent catheterisation, there was limited evidence suggesting that antibiotics reduced the rate of bacteriuria, both symptomatic and asymptomatic. There was weak evidence indicating that prophylactic antibiotics were associated with fewer cases of symptomatic bacteriuria. No eligible trials were identified that compared different routes of catheter insertion. The data from the eight trials evaluating various antibiotic policies were limited, particularly when intermittent catheterisation was considered separately from indwelling catheterisation. While there may be potential benefits to using antibiotic prophylaxis, these must be weighed against the risk of adverse effects, such as the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Unfortunately, the current body of evidence does not allow for reliable estimation of these risks.
